name: Palette Budget
summary: A design system should ship with ~5–8 core color tokens; exceeding ~10 distinct hex values almost always indicates duplication, not intentional variety.
description: Color palettes bloat silently. A new section needs a 'slightly darker border', a hover state gets a one-off tint, a shadow uses a novel rgba — and suddenly the page has 15 hex values, most of which are visually indistinguishable. A disciplined palette has a fixed budget: 1–2 brand colors, 1 accent, 3–5 neutral steps, and semantic states (success/warning/error/info). Everything else should be derived (opacity, mix) or reused. If you find yourself reaching for a new hex, the correct move is almost always to reuse an existing token.
implications: Define the full palette upfront as named tokens (brand, accent, neutral-50 through neutral-900, success, warning, error, info)
Cap distinct hex values at ~8–10 across the entire product surface
Derive variations through opacity (rgba) or color-mix() rather than new hex values
Use a single neutral scale for borders, dividers, muted text, and backgrounds — pick the closest step, don't invent a new one
Treat shadows as tokens too — define 2–4 elevation levels, not arbitrary rgba per component
When adding a section, audit existing tokens before introducing a new shade
violations: Three nearly-identical grays for borders (#e5e5e5), dividers (#e8e8e8), and muted backgrounds (#ececec)
One-off hover tints generated per-component instead of a systematic 'hover' modifier
Hardcoded rgba shadows that differ slightly across cards, modals, and dropdowns
Section-specific 'accent' colors that drift from the brand accent
More than 10 distinct hex values on a single page
Duplicating a token with a 1–2 point hex difference because 'this one needs to be slightly warmer'

name: Token Reuse Over Invention
summary: When a new UI element needs a color, reach for an existing token first; only invent a new one when no existing token is within ~5% perceptual distance.
description: Every new color in a system has a maintenance cost: it must be themed, tested for contrast, documented, and kept consistent across components. The default behavior when building a new section or component should be to pick the closest existing token, not to introduce a new shade. A useful heuristic: if a candidate new color is within ~5% perceptual distance (roughly ΔE < 5) of an existing token, use the existing one. Users will not perceive the difference, and the system stays coherent.
implications: Make the token list visible to designers and developers during component creation
Build linting that flags hardcoded hex values in components — force usage of named tokens
When in doubt, round to the nearest existing neutral step rather than inventing a new one
Document the intended use of each token (e.g., 'neutral-200 for subtle borders AND dividers AND disabled backgrounds') so reuse is the obvious path
Resist the urge to add 'just one more' shade for a specific component — that shade will spawn cousins
violations: Adding neutral-250 because neutral-200 felt 'a bit too light' for one specific card
Per-component color decisions made in isolation without checking the token list
Designers picking colors from a color picker instead of from the token palette
Developers writing inline hex values instead of referencing tokens
Multiple tokens that serve the same semantic purpose (e.g., 'border-default' and 'divider-line' both pointing to near-identical grays)

name: Palette Bloat Detection
summary: If a page uses more than ~10 distinct hex values, it almost certainly contains duplicated near-identical colors that should be consolidated.
description: Palette bloat is hard to see by eye because the duplicates are, by definition, visually similar. The fastest detection is mechanical: count distinct hex values (including rgba) across the rendered page. A well-systemized product surface lands at 8–10. Above 12 indicates drift. Common bloat sources: (1) slightly-different grays used for borders vs. dividers vs. muted text vs. disabled states, (2) one-off hover and active tints invented per-component, (3) hardcoded rgba shadow values that differ across elevations, (4) section-specific accent variations, (5) imported third-party components bringing their own color values. The fix is consolidation: pick the dominant value in each cluster and replace the rest.
implications: Add a build-time or CI check that counts distinct hex/rgba values per page and warns above a threshold (~10)
Periodically audit rendered pages with a color-extraction tool to catch drift
Cluster near-identical colors (ΔE < 5) and consolidate to a single token
Treat shadows and rgba overlays with the same scrutiny as solid colors — they bloat palettes too
When the count is high, look first at neutrals (borders, dividers, muted text) — that's where 60% of bloat lives
violations: Shipping a marketing page with 11+ distinct hex values
No automated detection — palette size is only noticed during occasional manual audits
Treating rgba and hex as separate palettes (they're not — they all contribute to perceived color count)
Consolidation deferred indefinitely because 'it's just a few extra grays'
